title: The self is never born
hookLine: Death's answer: the self is not born and does not die
carry: the self is not born and does not die
tomorrow: who's really steering? Death draws a chariot

cards: If you read the Gita with us, today may bring a jolt of recognition. There's a verse you've heard before, in chapter two, when Krishna first tells Arjuna that the self can't be killed.
Here it is again, almost word for word. Except now it isn't Krishna speaking on a battlefield. It's Death, speaking to a child.
Most scholars think the Gita drew on the Katha. Today Yama finally answers the question.

teach.h: NOT BORN, AND DOES NOT DIE.
teach.b: Yama says: the knowing self is not born, and does not die. It didn't come from anywhere, and it didn't become anyone. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient: it is not killed when the body is killed.
Then: if the killer thinks he kills, and the killed thinks he's killed, neither of them understands.

teach.h: IT DOES NOT KILL; IT IS NOT KILLED.
teach.b: This one does not kill, and is not killed. Those two verses reappear in the Gita, two nineteen and two twenty, with small changes.
So Death's answer to what happens when we die: the self you really are, the atman, was never born, so it can't die. The body ends; the self doesn't.
This is one of the deepest teachings in Hinduism, and it's why Hindu funerals speak of a body let go, not a person ended. Then Yama adds how this is known.
The self is smaller than the small and greater than the great, hidden in the heart of every creature.
It can't be gotten by lectures, or by brains, or by much learning.
It's gained by the one it chooses; to that one it reveals its own nature. Commentators read that line differently. Shankara hears the seeker choosing the self alone.
Theistic teachers like Ramanuja hear grace: the Lord chooses whom to reveal himself to.

teach.h: SMALLER THAN SMALL, GREATER THAN GREAT.
teach.b: Both schools agree on the next line: not the one who hasn't turned from wrong, not the restless, not the scattered, can reach it by cleverness. That's why the two paths matter.
Choosing the good over the pleasant isn't a rule for its own sake. It's what makes the mind quiet enough to notice what was never born.

how: Bhagavad Gita 2.20, which closely echoes Katha 1.2.18, is often recited at Hindu funerals and memorials as the teaching that the self, the atman, is not born and does not die.

o: reborn, coming back in a new life

p: the killer who thinks he kills

it appears earlier in the Katha, spoken by Death to Nachiketa.

not by lectures, brains or learning; by the one it chooses.

hidden in the heart of every creature.

games.q: Nachiketa asks what happens when a person dies. what does Death say?
o: 'the self is not born and does not die.'
games.why: the knowing self was never born, so it isn't killed when the body is. the Gita repeats it.

practice: Notice what in you has changed over the years: your body, your opinions, your face in photos. Then notice what hasn't, the plain sense of being here, aware, there at seven and here now, and rest in it for a few breaths.
If someone you love has died, you can hold them in mind too; this is the teaching many Hindu families lean on at a memorial.

wordCard.voice: Aja, unborn. The knowing self is not born, and does not die; it is not killed when the body is killed, unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient.

orig.note: Sanskrit: aja, unborn; Katha 1.2.18 calls the self unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient.

carryVoice: Your line: the self is not born and does not die. Even Death answered the boy in the end. See you tomorrow.
